title: Trump's Crypto Web
author: Kushal Pagarani
position: Chief Editor of the DESConomic Review
body:
INTRODUCTION

Cryptocurrencies are digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, a decentralised ledger that removes the need for banks or governments to verify transactions. Supporters see this as financial freedom, but the market is highly speculative and prone to abuse or corruption. This mix of excitement and risk means crypto can be extremely dangerous depending on how it is used. For teenagers and young investors especially, this makes crypto look both like a chance for fast profit and a trap waiting to happen.

THE RISKS OF CRYPTO

Contrary to traditional fiat currencies such as dollars or pounds, crypto coins are not backed by governments or central banks. This means their value can swing wildly in just hours, creating opportunities for massive gains but also devastating losses. Because regulation is still weak, scams and speculative bubbles are common, leaving inexperienced investors especially exposed. Stories of pump-and-dump schemes, hacked exchanges, and fake tokens appear frequently, showing how easy it is for people to be tricked. At the same time, the lack of consumer protection means that once money is lost, it is almost impossible to recover. These problems make crypto one of the riskiest financial experiments of the modern era.

HOW IT ALL STARTED

In January 2025, Trump launched his own meme coin, branded $TRUMP. It quickly surged in value and generated millions in trading fees. However, the hype left many small traders with significant losses once the price dropped, raising questions about who really benefited. Many people against it argued that while Trump and early investors made money, ordinary traders were left carrying heavy financial losses; online forums are even filled with posts from people claiming they lost savings, sparking anger at how easily hype can mislead.

Around the same time, Trump moved to appoint Paul Atkins, a supporter of cryptocurrency, as head of the SEC (the main U.S. financial regulator overseeing markets). Since the SEC is supposed to regulate the industry, the decision was seen as an attempt to put a crypto ally in charge of its oversight. This raised wider concerns about whether financial rules would be written to favour insiders instead of protecting the general public.

POTENTIAL CONCERNS

The Guardian said that Trump was hyping up his own coin at the same time as putting a pro-crypto ally in charge of regulation, which basically meant rules could be loosened in his favour. It suggested that Trump was shaping the system to benefit his own ventures rather than ensuring fair oversight. This gave the impression of a president more interested in boosting the price of his own coin than protecting citizens from risk.

POTENTIAL OPPORTUNITIES/REDEMPTION

Despite the backlash, Trump's crypto push may have had some unexpected upsides. By launching $TRUMP and openly promoting digital assets, he helped bring crypto into the mainstream. What was once a niche interest among tech enthusiasts suddenly became a topic of national debate, drawing attention from media outlets, regulators, and everyday citizens. This kind of visibility can accelerate innovation and force governments to take crypto seriously, potentially leading to clearer rules and safer markets.

At the same time, the coin's popularity gave retail investors a chance to participate in a financial movement often dominated by institutions. For some, it felt like a rare moment where ordinary people could get in early and profit from a trend before Wall Street did. While many lost money, others saw it as a form of economic empowerment, a way to challenge traditional finance and take control of their own investments.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • Allegations were made that regular people lost money on the $TRUMP coin, while insiders and trading platforms made millions. This created a widening gap between those with influence in the market and everyday citizens trying to participate. This is especially damaging because meme coins often attract younger traders with little experience, making them more vulnerable to sudden crashes.

  • Potentially, with a pro-crypto figure now leading the SEC, there are fears that oversight will be too soft, making it easier for scams to spread. Some experts warn that this could lead to long-term damage for trust in financial institutions and regulation itself.

  • An overlap between Trump's private money-making and his public role as president has made critics argue that he is using the office to benefit himself. It adds to growing debates about whether modern politics is being reshaped more by personal wealth than by public responsibility.

CONCLUSION

Trump's push into crypto shows how politics and personal business can become closely linked. From launching his own meme coin to putting crypto supporters in charge of regulation, it raises serious questions about whether he's using his position to benefit himself. Critics say it looks like he's more focused on boosting his own profits than protecting the public. However, others argue that by promoting crypto, he's helped bring it into the spotlight and forced governments to take it more seriously. That could lead to better rules and more awareness of the risks. Whether this turns into a scandal or becomes part of how modern politics works, it's already changed how people think about money, power, and leadership.

HAVE A THINK:

  • Should leaders be allowed to promote personal financial assets while in office?
  • Can cryptocurrency ever be safely regulated with insiders in charge?
  • Who protects ordinary investors when hype drives the market?

title: France's Economic Crisis
author: Yashas Hans
position: Chief Editor of the DESConomic Review
body:
INTRODUCTION

Once an economic powerhouse of Europe, France is dealing with a serious economic crisis. Its government owes a large amount of money, and there's even talk about needing help from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). But how did we get here? This crisis isn't just about numbers — it is a result of irresponsible spending and a paralysed parliament.

THE BASICS: HOW A COUNTRY'S ECONOMY WORKS

Every country earns money from taxes and spends it on things like schools, hospitals, roads, and helping people in need. If it spends more than it earns, it has a deficit. To cover that, it borrows money, which adds to its debt. France's debt is now over €3.3 trillion — more than 114% of its GDP (the total value of everything made and sold in France in a year). That's a record high, and it's growing fast because of past events like the COVID-19 pandemic and high energy prices after Russia's war in Ukraine began in 2022.

HOW DID IT GET THIS BAD?

For decades, France has spent heavily on public services — great healthcare, free schools, and strong worker protections. But it hasn't balanced its budget since 1974, meaning it always spends more than it collects in taxes. Pensions alone take up 15% of GDP, higher than many other countries. During tough times like the pandemic, France borrowed even more to keep businesses and people afloat.

Now, with slow economic growth of only 0.6% to 0.8% expected for 2025, paying it back is a serious challenge. Unemployment sits at 7.9%, and exports — things like wine and cars — are being hurt by possible new U.S. tariffs under President Trump.

POLITICAL PARALYSIS

Politics is making everything worse. President Emmanuel Macron dissolved parliament in July 2024 hoping for a stronger majority. Instead, no group won a clear majority, leaving the left and right blocking his centrist plans at every turn. In August 2025, a new prime minister, François Bayrou, took over — but his government immediately faced a confidence vote on September 8, 2025, with opponents from both sides threatening to block the budget.

THE BUDGET CRISIS

France's deficit sits at around 5.4% to 5.8% of GDP — well above the EU's 3% rule. Bayrou proposed cutting €44 billion in spending and raising some taxes, including scrapping two public holidays and reducing healthcare costs. The public is furious. Unions planned nationwide protests from September 10, 2025, fearing job losses and higher living costs. It echoes the Yellow Vest protests of 2018, which began over fuel taxes and quickly turned into widespread riots.

MARKETS AND CREDIT RATINGS

Markets are nervous. France sells bonds — essentially IOUs — to borrow money, and the interest rates on those bonds have jumped sharply. Ten-year bonds are at 3.5%, and 30-year bonds hit 4.42%, the highest in 14 years. Alarmingly, French rates are now close to those of Greece, which went through a devastating crisis in 2010. On September 19, 2025, the ratings agency Fitch downgraded France's debt, making future borrowing even more expensive.

COULD THE IMF STEP IN?

The IMF is like a global emergency bank — it lends money to struggling countries, but with strict conditions such as major spending cuts. In August 2025, France's Finance Minister Éric Lombard warned that an IMF bailout was a risk if things don't improve, though he later said it isn't happening yet. France can still borrow from markets, unlike Greece in 2010 or the UK in the 1970s when they truly ran out of options. Most experts believe that if help is needed, it would more likely come from European mechanisms like the ESM or the ECB — not the IMF.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • Debt payments could hit €100 billion by 2029 — more than France's entire defence or education budget. Ordinary people may face higher taxes, fewer public holidays, and cuts to schools and healthcare.

  • A French crisis would shake the euro and send ripples across Europe, particularly to neighbours like Germany who are closely tied to France's economy.

  • Political instability is growing. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is waiting in the wings, and a worsening crisis could hand her the power she needs if voters blame Macron for the fallout.

CONCLUSION

France isn't doomed — it remains one of Europe's largest economies with high productivity and strong living standards. But it needs urgent political unity to pass a budget and begin fixing the deficit. Without it, the crisis will only deepen. The ECB could step in to stabilise markets, but that won't solve the underlying problem. France's story is a reminder that even the wealthiest nations cannot spend beyond their means forever — and that balancing the books, however painful, is unavoidable in the end.

HAVE A THINK:

  • Should governments keep borrowing to protect public services, or is cutting spending the only responsible option?
  • Is it fair for ordinary people to pay for a crisis caused by years of political decisions they had little say in?
  • What lessons can other countries learn from France before they face a similar situation?

title: Should the UK government introduce a “robot tax”?
author: Amay Gambhir
body:
INTRODUCTION

With the rapid advancement of technology and artificial intelligence reshaping the UK economy, daily tasks once done by humans are increasingly being handed over to machines. From automated warehouses to robots in the hospitality industry, the pace of change has caught many off guard. While automation promises higher productivity and long-term economic growth, it also presents a serious challenge to the UK's tax and welfare systems — both of which rely on income generated through human labour. This raises an important question: should the UK government introduce a "robot tax"?

THE RISE OF AUTOMATION IN THE UK

In today's UK economy, automation is part of everyday life. From robotics to AI and machine learning, businesses are steadily replacing routine human tasks with machines and software — especially in logistics, manufacturing, retail, and professional services. High-skilled workers who manage these technologies often benefit through higher wages. Low-skilled workers, however, face greater job insecurity and wage stagnation, deepening income inequality over time. This has played out against a backdrop of already weak productivity growth and regional inequality, making the policy dilemma even harder: how do you encourage innovation while making sure the costs of technological change don't fall hardest on the most vulnerable?

THE TAX PROBLEM

A major concern surrounding automation is its impact on government revenue. The UK tax system relies heavily on income tax and National Insurance contributions — both directly tied to human employment. When workers are replaced by machines, tax revenue falls even if firms become more profitable. Crucially, employers pay National Insurance on wages, but no equivalent tax exists when a firm replaces workers with machines. As Bogenschneider (2018) argues, the system should be at least neutral between robot and human workers, so that automation decisions are driven by genuine efficiency rather than tax incentives. Without reform, the government risks a steady decline in revenue at exactly the moment when demand for public services — retraining programmes, welfare support — is rising.

THE CASE FOR A ROBOT TAX

Supporters argue that a robot tax could help stabilise public finances while promoting fairness in the labour market. By requiring firms that benefit from automation to contribute more to the tax base, the government could offset losses in income tax and National Insurance revenues. Those funds could then be invested in reskilling, education, and social welfare — helping displaced workers transition into new roles. There is also a broader point: firms that profit from automation operate within societies that provide infrastructure, education systems, and legal protections. A robot tax would be a way for those firms to contribute to the social costs their decisions create, and would push companies to automate for the right reasons — productivity gains — rather than simply because machines are more tax-efficient than people.

THE CASE AGAINST

Despite these arguments, a robot tax is not straightforward. The first problem is definition — automation exists on a spectrum, from basic software to complex machinery, and taxing "robots" directly risks creating serious legal ambiguity. There are also concerns that such a tax could discourage innovation and damage the UK's international competitiveness. If firms face higher costs for adopting modern technology, they may delay investment or relocate to countries with more favourable conditions. In the long run, this could harm productivity growth and ultimately reduce wages and living standards — the very outcomes a robot tax is meant to prevent.

A SMARTER APPROACH

Rather than taxing robots directly, a more effective solution would be to reform existing labour and corporate taxation to address the consequences of automation. One option is to adjust employer National Insurance contributions so that firms which significantly reduce their workforce through automation contribute more to public finances. This shifts the focus from the technology itself to its impact on employment — avoiding the definitional problems while still correcting the fiscal imbalance. Firms would not be penalised for using technology unless it leads to substantial labour displacement, preserving the incentive to innovate responsibly.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • Automation disproportionately affects low-skilled workers, who are often least able to retrain without state support. Meanwhile, wealth generated through automation tends to flow to firm owners and highly skilled professionals, widening the inequality gap further.

  • A decline in income tax and National Insurance revenue, if left unaddressed, could put serious pressure on the NHS, welfare, and public services at exactly the time more people need them.

  • Without intervention, rising child poverty and regional inequality in the UK are likely to worsen — making tax reform not just desirable, but necessary for the long-term health of the economy.

CONCLUSION

The question of whether the UK should introduce a robot tax doesn't have a simple yes or no answer. Taxing robots directly risks discouraging innovation and creating legal confusion. But doing nothing — maintaining a tax system that already implicitly favours automation by taxing labour far more heavily than capital — is equally problematic. The smarter path is a reform of tax policy that focuses on the impact of automation rather than the technology itself. If done well, it can protect public revenues, tackle inequality, and ensure that the gains from automation are shared more widely across society. As machines reshape the economy, the real challenge isn't stopping progress — it's managing it responsibly.

HAVE A THINK:

  • Is it fair that companies can replace workers with machines without paying any equivalent to the National Insurance they saved?
  • Could a robot tax end up hurting the workers it's trying to protect by slowing down economic growth?
  • Who should decide how the money from a robot tax is spent — and how do we make sure it actually reaches those who need it most?

title: Uber in Dubai: High Prices in a Controlled Market
author: Ilyaas Mirza
body:
INTRODUCTION

If you've taken an Uber in Dubai before, you would understand that the experience is fluid and more of a luxury than a normal taxi. However, consumers — including myself — have noticed increasingly high fares on domestic trips, and it begs the question: why are Uber fares consistently higher than expected? This has led me to question whether prices are driven less by corporate greed and more by regulation, cost structure, and consumer behaviour. The argument here is that Uber isn't charging extortionate fares due to market failure — but rather because of the very specific conditions that shape how it operates in Dubai.

MARKET STRUCTURE AND REGULATION

In Dubai, transport — public and private — is regulated by the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA), which plans transportation in a carefully curated way to ensure fluid movement across the city and maximise long-term efficiency as Dubai's population grows.

Uber in Dubai also operates very differently from other regions. Rather than an open-gig platform, it functions as a connector between RTA-licensed limousine drivers working through registered companies — closer to sub-contracting than the freelance model seen elsewhere. This creates relatively high barriers to entry, restricting supply. In a market with substantial demand and limited supply, Uber can set higher prices and operate close to a profit-maximising equilibrium. Even during quieter periods when supply may exceed demand, prices remain unexpectedly high.

COST STRUCTURE

Running Uber in Dubai comes with far higher fixed and variable costs than in most other regions. Drivers must be employed through registered companies, requiring commercial licences, and startup costs are steep. Vehicles are of a significantly higher standard too — at the lowest tier, a standard UberX in Dubai is likely to be a Lexus, a level of comfort that would sit at the Comfort or Black category in Europe or the US, at a much higher price point. Insurance costs also fall on the companies rather than individual drivers, adding further pressure.

All of this results in cost-push inflation — as operating costs rise, the supply curve shifts left, pushing the market equilibrium to a new point where prices are higher. Firms need those elevated prices to maintain the incentive to supply at all.

DEMAND REMAINS HIGH DESPITE PRICES

Despite the high fares, consumers continue to use Uber daily. In the first half of 2024 alone, over 55.7 million taxi trips were taken in Dubai, with Uber contributing significantly to that figure. Consumers keep coming back because of convenience, safety features, and seamless app-based payment — all of which make it easy to justify the cost. Tourists without private vehicles often default to Uber simply because they already know the brand. Dubai's population also tends to have higher disposable incomes, meaning the proportion of income spent on a ride is far smaller than it would be elsewhere — helping explain why demand is relatively inelastic.

COMPETITION AND MARKET POWER

The Dubai taxi market is best described as an oligopoly, dominated by Uber and Careem, a regional rival. New platforms have entered the market but have struggled to pull customers away from the established players, resorting to unsustainable discounts of 30–50% for new users — a model that cannot last in a high-cost operating environment.

Government RTA taxis do exist and are significantly cheaper, but they are widely perceived as less comfortable and carry a less prestigious image — with commercial advertising on the exterior reinforcing a sense of being a budget option. This perception gap allows Uber to maintain its premium positioning without serious competitive pressure from below.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • High barriers to entry limit competition, meaning consumers have little real alternative if they want the convenience and comfort Uber offers. This gives Uber and Careem considerable pricing power with little accountability to bring fares down.

  • Relatively inelastic demand means price increases are absorbed rather than resisted — which reduces the market pressure that would normally keep prices in check, and risks making premium transport inaccessible for lower-income residents.

  • The regulatory framework, while designed to ensure quality and safety, inadvertently locks in high prices by restricting supply. Well-intentioned policy can have unintended consequences for affordability.

CONCLUSION

Uber's high prices in Dubai are not evidence of market failure or corporate greed. They reflect a regulated transport market where supply is deliberately controlled, drivers face high fixed costs, and service quality is prioritised. Consumers continue to pay because convenience and reliability outweigh price concerns — and because the demographics of Dubai mean many can afford to. In that sense, Uber's pricing in Dubai is a textbook illustration of how well-designed regulation shapes markets, balancing service standards, driver welfare, and consumer choice — even when the result is fares that feel steep.

HAVE A THINK:

  • Is it fair that regulation designed to protect quality and safety ends up making transport less affordable for lower-income residents?
  • Should governments intervene when an oligopoly like Uber and Careem faces so little real competition?
  • Does inelastic demand let companies off the hook for high prices, or does it simply reflect what consumers genuinely value?

title: How does the West End shape the UK economy?
author: Sarah Habib
body:
INTRODUCTION

If you have ever walked down the streets of London's West End, you would know there's always a buzzing crowd at every corner waiting to burst through the doors of every building containing an amazing theatre show. The streets are decorated with large posters, filled with some of the most popular performances in the world — it's a magical place to be. However, the West End isn't only a place of unforgettable performances. It is also a powerful economic engine for the UK economy. Beyond the stage and the glamour that surrounds it, it holds a serious and large impact on jobs, tourism, business, and the UK's global reputation. The West End doesn't just entertain the nation — it helps fuel it.

A TOURIST MAGNET

London is one of the most visited cities in the world, and a large part of that is because people want to experience world-class theatre at one of the premier entertainment districts on the planet. For many tourists, watching a West End show is as essential to their trip as visiting Big Ben.

This is where the multiplier effect comes in. Tourists don't just buy a ticket and leave — after a show, they spend money on hotels, restaurants, transportation, souvenirs, and shopping, creating further income that flows through the wider economy. The West End generates approximately £51.25 billion in Gross Value Added (GVA) and accounts for around 3% of the nation's total economic output. Through ticket sales and the employment of artists and technical staff, it directly boosts consumption — a key component of aggregate demand — and in turn increases UK GDP.

HOW IT AFFECTS UNEMPLOYMENT

One of the biggest strengths of the West End is its impact on employment. Because the industry is highly labour intensive, it opens up a wide variety of roles — from performers and directors to designers, technicians, and management — creating significant demand for labour across many different skill sets.

This increased demand can raise workers' bargaining power, potentially leading to higher wages. Higher wages mean greater purchasing power and consumer confidence, which leads to an increase in consumption across the broader economy. Since aggregate demand is calculated as consumption + investment + government spending + (exports − imports), a rise in consumption drives up aggregate demand and, with it, GDP.

THE CIRCULAR FLOW OF INCOME

The circular flow of income is an economic model that illustrates how money, resources, and goods move between households and firms — and the West End is a clear example of it in action. It begins when individuals purchase show tickets, generating revenue for theatres. That revenue is then used to pay the factors of production: wages for performers, management, design teams, and technicians. Those workers spend their disposable income on goods and services, injecting money back into the economy and increasing its overall size.

In economics, injections — government spending, investment, and exports — add money into the economy, while leakages — savings, taxes, and imports — take money out. When injections exceed leakages, aggregate demand rises, stimulating economic expansion and boosting national income.

A NEVER-ENDING CYCLE OF DEMAND

Another key economic concept visible in the West End is price elasticity of demand — how responsive consumers are to a change in price. Many of the West End's most well-known shows have price inelastic demand, meaning that even as ticket prices rise, demand stays largely unchanged. Because these performances are unique, prestigious, and praised globally, audiences — tourists especially — are willing to pay a premium, giving businesses the advantage of setting high prices without losing customers.

However, this doesn't apply equally across the board. Smaller and newer shows often face elastic demand, where even a modest price increase can cause a significant drop in sales, as audiences may choose a cheaper alternative or decide not to attend at all. This creates a clear divide between established productions with loyal, price-insensitive audiences and newer shows that must compete much harder for every seat.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • The West End's multiplier effect means that every pound spent on a theatre ticket generates far more economic activity across hotels, restaurants, transport, and retail — amplifying its contribution to GDP well beyond the box office alone.

  • As a labour-intensive industry, it plays an important role in reducing unemployment and raising wages in sectors that might otherwise struggle, supporting households and boosting consumer spending across London and beyond.

  • The divide between price inelastic blockbusters and price elastic newer shows creates an uneven playing field, where smaller productions face a far harder time surviving — potentially limiting the diversity and creativity of the West End's offering over time.

CONCLUSION

The West End is far more than a collection of dazzling performances. It is a significant driver of the UK economy, generating billions in output, supporting thousands of jobs, and attracting millions of tourists whose spending ripples outward through the wider economy. Through the multiplier effect, the circular flow of income, and the power of inelastic demand, it demonstrates how culture and economics are deeply intertwined. Protecting and investing in the West End isn't just about preserving an art form — it's about sustaining one of the UK's most valuable economic assets.

HAVE A THINK:

  • Should the government invest more in supporting smaller West End productions, or should the market decide which shows survive?
  • Is it fair that tourists are effectively subsidising an industry that many ordinary UK residents can no longer afford to attend?
  • Could the economic model of the West End be replicated in other UK cities, or is London's appeal simply too unique to copy?

title: How should the government balance the goals of reducing inequality and promoting economic growth?
author: Amay Gambhir
body:
INTRODUCTION

Governments have many economic goals: a stable balance of payments, low inflation, low unemployment, and economic growth. One of the most important is promoting growth — increasing the value of goods and services produced in a country — because it can lead to higher living standards and greater employment. Another key aim is reducing inequality, the gap between rich and poor. Countries like India illustrate this tension starkly, where some of the world's wealthiest individuals live alongside millions in poverty. Normally, governments struggle to achieve both goals at the same time. This article argues that sustainable growth actually depends on reducing inequality — through education, progressive taxation, and redistribution — and that while these policies may slow growth in the short run, they strengthen both equality and productivity in the long run.

INVESTING IN EDUCATION

Investing in high-quality education is one of the most impactful ways to reduce inequality. By subsidising education and training, governments can help lower-income workers gain skills that lead to better-paid jobs, narrowing the inequality gap over time. As the OECD (2021) notes, early investment in education systems can boost productivity significantly. This connects to the work of economist Robert Lucas (1998), who argued that education directly increases productivity in the long run.

The Nordic model offers a real-world example: countries with strong, well-funded education systems consistently achieve both high GDP per capita and relatively low inequality — demonstrating that the two goals can coexist. Beyond traditional schooling, reducing digital inequality is increasingly important. As technology becomes central to employment and productivity, investing in digital skills programmes gives low-income students the tools to compete in future technology-driven markets.

Critically, education spending should not just be about how much is spent, but where. Targeted investment in lower-income areas will do far more to close skill gaps than pouring resources into already well-funded schools. In the short run, this spending may reduce what the government can invest elsewhere — such as infrastructure — but the long-run returns in productivity and reduced inequality make it worthwhile.

TAX AND REDISTRIBUTION

There are two main approaches to income taxation. A regressive tax charges the same amount regardless of earnings, meaning lower-income workers pay a higher proportion of their income — which worsens inequality. A progressive tax, by contrast, increases the rate as income rises, ensuring those who earn more contribute a higher percentage — a fairer outcome for lower-paid workers.

Economist Thomas Piketty (2014) showed that without redistribution, the gap between rich and poor will simply keep growing: capital accumulates at the top while those at the bottom fall further behind. Progressive taxation allows governments to fund unemployment benefits and cash transfer programmes — such as Brazil's Bolsa Família — which increase disposable income for lower-income households, boost consumption, and shift aggregate demand to the right, driving economic growth.

Some economists argue that high taxes discourage entrepreneurship and could push wealthy individuals and businesses towards low-tax countries. However, the OECD (2015) found that moderate redistribution has a net positive effect on economic performance. The key is balance — reducing inequality without taxing to the point where incentives for innovation and investment disappear.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • Without investment in education and digital skills, low-income workers risk being permanently left behind in a technology-driven economy, locking inequality in place across generations rather than reducing it.

  • Progressive taxation and targeted welfare programmes, when well-designed, increase disposable incomes at the lower end of the economy — boosting consumption, raising aggregate demand, and generating growth that benefits everyone.

  • Getting the balance wrong — taxing too heavily or spending without regard for quality and targeting — can slow growth, deter investment, and ultimately reduce the government revenue needed to fund the very programmes designed to reduce inequality.

CONCLUSION

Reducing inequality and promoting economic growth are not competing goals — they are deeply connected. Education, progressive taxation, and redistribution form a framework where fairness supports productivity rather than hindering it. As more people gain skills and access to better-paying jobs, labour productivity rises, consumption increases, and the economy expands in a way that benefits a wider share of the population. In the long run, governments should aim for steady, inclusive growth — not just chasing headline GDP figures, but ensuring the gains from growth are shared broadly. A fairer economy is not just the morally right outcome; it is also the economically smart one.

HAVE A THINK:

  • Can a country ever truly achieve both rapid economic growth and low inequality at the same time, or does one always come at the cost of the other?
  • Is progressive taxation the fairest way to fund public services, or does it risk punishing success and discouraging ambition?
  • Who is responsible for reducing inequality — governments through policy, businesses through fair pay, or individuals through education and effort?

title: How Effective Is a National Minimum Wage in High Income Countries?
author: Ilias Vougiouklakis
body:
INTRODUCTION

A national minimum wage is one of the most widely used policy tools for protecting low-paid workers. In high-income countries, where labour markets are relatively formalised and social protection systems are well developed, the question is not whether minimum wages matter — but how far they can go in reducing inequality, supporting living standards, and shaping employment outcomes. Evidence from international organisations and recent research points to a clear conclusion: minimum wages are generally effective at improving earnings for the lowest-paid, but their broader impact depends heavily on economic conditions, enforcement, and the level at which they are set.

RAISING THE FLOOR: WAGES AND LIVING STANDARDS

High-income countries with national minimum wages have seen these policies play a stabilising role in wage dynamics. Real statutory minimum wages in nearly all OECD countries were higher in early 2025 than in early 2021 — even after the inflation surge that followed the pandemic. This suggests that minimum wages helped preserve purchasing power for low-income workers during a period of significant economic stress.

Trade unions and labour organisations also emphasise the role of minimum wages in ensuring adequate living standards. According to global wage surveys, they are seen as a vital measure for preventing in-work poverty and countering long-term declines in real wages relative to the cost of living. In high-income contexts, where costs are high and inequality is often entrenched, a well-set minimum wage can serve as a foundation for maintaining a basic standard of living for those at the bottom of the income distribution.

INEQUALITY AND POVERTY: GAINS WITH LIMITS

Research on high-income countries shows that minimum wages can reduce income inequality, particularly by lifting the earnings of workers living below the living wage. Evidence from European Union countries indicates that minimum wages help narrow wage gaps and reduce inequality within the labour market.

However, the relationship is not straightforward. A recent cross-country study covering 31 nations between 2001 and 2021 found that while initial increases in minimum wages reduce poverty and inequality, the marginal benefits diminish as the minimum wage rises further. At higher levels, additional increases may have limited or even counterproductive effects — firms face rising production costs and may no longer be able to sustain their lowest-paid employees, potentially worsening unemployment and pushing people onto government benefits. This suggests minimum wages are most effective when set at moderate levels: high enough to lift incomes, but not so high that they disrupt labour demand.

EMPLOYMENT EFFECTS: SMALL AND MANAGEABLE

One of the most debated questions is whether minimum wages reduce employment. In high-income countries, the evidence is often inconsistent, reflecting the many other factors at play in any given economy. Research across European countries suggests that employment impacts vary by sector and region rather than being uniformly negative. Sectors with thin profit margins or high concentrations of low-wage labour — such as hospitality, retail, and agriculture — may face more pressure. But across high-income economies, minimum wage increases have generally not led to large-scale job losses.

Several factors explain this resilience. High productivity levels allow firms to absorb cost increases more easily, and low-income households tend to have a much higher marginal propensity to consume — meaning the boost to consumer spending from higher wages can offset the pressure on firms' costs. The overall picture is that minimum wages tend to have limited negative employment effects, especially when increases are gradual, predictable, and aligned with broader economic conditions.

IMPACTS

The effects are significant:

  • Minimum wages have helped preserve the purchasing power of low-income workers even during periods of high inflation, acting as a buffer against the worst effects of rising living costs on the most vulnerable households.

  • While effective at narrowing wage gaps, minimum wages alone cannot eliminate poverty — particularly in households relying on part-time work or multiple earners, where the structural causes of low income go beyond the hourly wage rate.

  • Sectors with low profit margins remain vulnerable to disruption when minimum wages rise sharply, risking localised job losses that disproportionately affect the very workers the policy is designed to protect.

CONCLUSION

The evidence is clear: national minimum wages are generally effective in high-income countries at raising low wages, reducing inequality, and supporting living standards — with limited adverse effects on employment when designed carefully. But their effectiveness is not guaranteed. It depends on appropriate wage-setting mechanisms that track productivity and living costs, strong enforcement to tackle non-compliance, and complementary policies — such as tax credits, childcare support, and retraining programmes — that help translate higher wages into real improvements in household wellbeing. A minimum wage raises the floor, but it cannot by itself reshape the entire wage structure or eradicate poverty. It is best understood as one essential component of a much broader strategy for fair and sustainable growth.

HAVE A THINK:

  • At what point does raising the minimum wage stop helping low-paid workers and start hurting them?
  • Should the minimum wage be set nationally, or adjusted by region to reflect local costs of living and economic conditions?
  • Can a minimum wage ever be enough on its own, or does reducing poverty always require a wider package of support?

title: Alfred Marshall
author: Aamir Boriawala
body:
WHO IS ALFRED MARSHALL?

Alfred Marshall, born in London in 1842, was the dominant figure in British economics from the late 19th century until his death in 1924, a period during which British economic thought shaped much of the world. Educated at St. John's College, Cambridge, Marshall defied his family's wish for him to enter the clergy and instead pursued mathematics before turning to economics. His work laid the foundations of modern microeconomics — the study of individual markets, firms, and consumer behaviour.

Marshall is widely regarded as the father of neoclassical economics. His work blended classical ideas with new insights into market behaviour, shaping how economists study individual markets, consumer decisions, and price formation. His clear diagrams, analytical frameworks, and emphasis on real-world observation made economic theory more accessible and practical.

KEY CONTRIBUTIONS

Supply & Demand: The Scissor Analogy

Marshall argued that prices are determined jointly by supply and demand, famously comparing the two forces to the blades of a pair of scissors — each essential in determining equilibrium. Modern economists still begin any price analysis by examining shifts in these two curves, a direct legacy of Marshall's framework.

Price Elasticity of Demand

He introduced the concept of elasticity, measuring how sensitive buyers are to price changes. This remains a central tool for understanding consumer behaviour and firm pricing strategies.

Consumer & Producer Surplus

Marshall developed the concepts of consumer and producer surplus to measure the benefits enjoyed by buyers and sellers. These ideas became the foundation of welfare economics, allowing economists to evaluate how taxes, subsidies, and policies affect overall well-being.

Short Run vs Long Run

To explain how markets adjust over time, Marshall distinguished between three periods: - Market period: supply fixed - Short period: labour and inputs can adjust - Long period: capital and technology can change

This framework remains central to production theory and market analysis.

Economic Dynamics & Evolution

Although he used mathematical tools from classical mechanics, Marshall believed the economy was ultimately an evolving system — "economic biology," as he called it — where technology, institutions, and preferences change over time.

OPPOSITIONS TO HIS THEORIES

Economists later challenged Marshall's models for being too simplified. Critics argued that his smooth supply and demand curves did not fully capture the complexity of real markets, especially under uncertainty or rapid technological change. General-equilibrium theorists claimed his focus on individual markets ignored how interconnected the economy truly is. Keynes, one of his own students, questioned Marshall's belief that markets naturally adjust to equilibrium, arguing instead that wages and prices can be slow to change, requiring government intervention during recessions. Others believed Marshall's static diagrams could not reflect the evolving nature of economies, despite his own suggestion that economics should move toward an "economic biology."

HOW HIS WORK IS APPLIED TODAY

Marshall's ideas remain central to modern economics. Businesses use elasticity to set prices and predict consumer responses, while governments rely on consumer and producer surplus to evaluate taxes, subsidies, and policy impacts. His distinctions between short-run and long-run production guide firms' investment and planning decisions. Regulators apply Marshallian principles when assessing competition and market power, and his supply-and-demand framework continues to shape economic modelling and education worldwide.

title: John Maynard Keynes
author: Aamir Boriawala
body:
WHO IS JOHN MAYNARD KEYNES?

John Maynard Keynes, one of the most influential economists of the 20th century, was born in 1883 in Cambridge, England. Educated at Eton and later at Cambridge University, he became a central figure in redefining modern macroeconomics. Keynes is best known for challenging classical economic assumptions and for developing a framework that explained how governments could stabilise economies during downturns. His ideas reshaped global economic policy and remain foundational today.

THE GENERAL THEORY OF EMPLOYMENT, INTEREST AND MONEY (1936)

Keynes argued that economies are not always self-correcting. Instead of relying on free markets to restore full employment, he believed that insufficient demand could trap an economy in prolonged recession. His work introduced concepts such as aggregate demand, the multiplier effect, and the importance of government spending to stimulate economic activity.

KEYNESIAN ECONOMICS

Keynes proposed that during recessions, governments should intervene through fiscal policy — raising public spending or cutting taxes — to boost demand. He rejected the classical view that markets naturally return to equilibrium, insisting that active policy is essential to prevent mass unemployment and economic stagnation. His ideas laid the groundwork for modern macroeconomic management and institutions such as the IMF and World Bank.

KEYNESIAN ECONOMIC PRINCIPLES

1. Aggregate Demand: Keynes argued that total spending in the economy determines overall output and employment. When demand falls, economies can enter long periods of stagnation.

2. Multiplier Effect: An increase in government spending leads to a more than proportional increase in national income. This happens because one person's spending becomes another person's income, creating a chain reaction of economic activity.

3. Fiscal Policy Intervention: Keynes believed governments must actively manage the economy. During recessions, higher public spending or tax cuts can boost demand; during booms, governments should reduce spending to prevent inflation.

4. Liquidity Trap: In severe downturns, cutting interest rates may not stimulate borrowing or investment. Keynes argued that monetary policy alone is sometimes ineffective, making fiscal policy essential.

OPPOSITIONS TO HIS THEORIES

Monetarists, led by Milton Friedman, argued that Keynes underestimated the power of monetary policy and that excessive government spending leads to inflation. They believed controlling the money supply is the key to stable growth.

New Classical economists criticised Keynes for assuming markets are slow to adjust. They argued that individuals form rational expectations, making government intervention less effective.

A major historical challenge to Keynesianism came in the 1970s, when economies experienced stagflation — high inflation and unemployment simultaneously — something Keynesian models struggled to explain.

HOW IS THIS APPLIED TODAY?

Today, Keynes's ideas remain central to how governments respond to economic crises. Countries use fiscal stimulus packages — increased public spending, tax cuts, and direct support — to boost demand during recessions. This approach was widely adopted during the 2008 Financial Crisis and again during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Keynesian thinking also underpins automatic stabilisers such as unemployment benefits and progressive taxation, which naturally increase or decrease with the business cycle to smooth economic fluctuations.

Institutions like the IMF and World Bank were founded on Keynesian principles, promoting global financial stability and supporting countries facing economic downturns.

Modern examples include governments funding infrastructure projects to create jobs or providing subsidies to industries during downturns to prevent mass unemployment — clear reflections of Keynes's belief in active economic management.
